**RE: Appeal of adverse benefit determination dated 2026-08-11**
**Member:** Taylor Carter | **Member ID:** W508456906
**Reference number:** POC-A755F8592E-91154
**Service denied:** Shoulder labral / instability repair, CPT 29806
**Governing policy:** Carelon Clinical Appropriateness Guidelines: Joint Surgery (MSK02-1125.1), https://guidelines.carelonmedicalbenefitsmanagement.com/joint-surgery-2025-11-15/

---

Dear Appeals Reviewer,

I am appealing the denial of prior authorization for the shoulder labral/instability repair (CPT 29806) requested by my surgeon, Dr. Duval, MD, orthopedic surgery. The notice dated 2026-08-11 states that the imaging findings submitted do not support the medical necessity of the requested procedure. I am asking the plan to reconsider that decision, because the records in my file match the plan's own published criteria point by point — including the imaging criterion the denial relies on.

I have set out below the plan's criteria in its own words, followed by what my records show.

## 1. The imaging criterion — the stated reason for the denial

The plan's guideline states:

> "MRI demonstrates at least ONE of the following: A labral lesion consistent with the clinical instability Hill-Sachs lesion Capsular tear Capsular redundancy with clinical multidirectional instability"

My MR arthrogram of the shoulder dated 2026-07-08 shows an anteroinferior labral tear (Bankart lesion) with a small Hill-Sachs lesion, glenoid bone loss under 10 percent, and an intact rotator cuff. That is a labral lesion, and it is on the anteroinferior side — the same direction as my three anterior dislocations and my positive apprehension and relocation tests. It is also, separately, a Hill-Sachs lesion. The policy asks for at least one of the listed findings; my imaging documents two of them.

The guideline also states:

> "Imaging report . The provider shall submit a detailed imaging report for studies obtained within the past 12 months. In the absence of a detailed report, the provider may submit a report from an independent radiologist."

My study was obtained on 2026-07-08, well within twelve months of the request and of this appeal. If the imaging report did not reach the reviewer, or if the copy in the file was incomplete, I ask that the plan tell me so specifically and accept a further copy rather than deny the surgery on that basis. I am requesting that the full MR arthrogram report be re-sent with this appeal by [imaging facility / ordering office — to be confirmed].

## 2. History of dislocation or subluxation

> "History of a shoulder dislocation or recurrent subluxation"

My records document 24 months of recurrent episodes of shoulder instability with apprehension, and three anterior dislocations since my symptoms began. The most recent dislocation was reduced in the emergency department.

## 3. Effect on daily activities

> "Shoulder pain and/or instability which interferes with age-appropriate activities of daily living"

The records state that I avoid overhead reaching and that I cannot return to my work lifting.

The guideline also states:

> "Reporting symptom severity – Severity of pain and its associated impact on activities of daily living (ADLs) and instrumental ADLs (IADLs) are key factors in determining the need for intervention. For purposes of this guideline, significant pain and functional impairment refer to pain rated at least 3 out of 10 in intensity and associated with inability to perform ADLs and/or IADLs."

The functional side of that definition is documented in my chart as described above. For the numeric pain rating, I ask the plan to refer to the rating recorded in my office and physical therapy notes: [pain score as documented in the chart, with date — to be completed from the records]. If the plan believes a pain rating is missing from what it received, I ask that it identify that gap in writing so it can be supplied.

## 4. Physical examination

> "Physical exam consistent with symptomatic glenohumeral instability (e.g., apprehension, relocation, load and shift)"

My examination documents positive apprehension and relocation tests and increased anterior translation on load-and-shift testing, with full strength. Those are the three examples the policy itself names.

## 5. Conservative management

> "Failure of at least 12 weeks of conservative management (unless history of traumatic dislocation and multiple dislocations during management)*"

I completed supervised physical therapy from 2026-04-03 to 2026-06-26 — twelve weeks — with 16 visits completed, focused on rotator cuff and scapular stabilizer strengthening with activity modification. This is documented in the physical therapy discharge note.

> "Conservative management 1 must include a combination of strategies to reduce inflammation, alleviate pain, and correct underlying dysfunction, including physical therapy AND at least ONE complementary conservative treatment strategy."

I had physical therapy, plus activity modification, plus NSAIDs for four months during flares. I did not have an injection because, as the records note, injection is not indicated for instability.

> "Failure of conservative management requires ALL the following: Patient has completed a full course of conservative management (as defined above) for the current episode of care Worsening of or no significant improvement in signs and/or symptoms upon clinical reevaluation More invasive forms of therapy are being considered"

Taking those in order: I completed the full 12-week course for this episode of care; on reevaluation my apprehension, relocation and load-and-shift findings remained positive and my instability persisted, which is why my surgeon documented that surgery is needed; and the more invasive option now under consideration is the requested repair itself.

> "Documentation of compliance with a plan of therapy that includes elements from these areas is required where conservative management is appropriate."

My 16 completed visits over the full 12-week course, recorded in the discharge note, document that compliance. The date of my post-therapy reevaluation visit is [date of clinical reevaluation visit — to be completed from the records].

The guideline also provides:

> "Clinical reevaluation – In most cases, reevaluation should include a physical examination. Direct contact by other methods, such as telephone communication or electronic messaging, may substitute for in-person evaluation when circumstances preclude an office visit."

My reevaluation included a physical examination, as the policy prefers.

## 6. A note on the criteria I was given

One of the plan's provisions reads:

> "Documentation supporting medical necessity and a clearly stated plan of care should be submitted at the time of the request and must include the following components:"

That sentence introduces a list of required components, and I do not have the full list in front of me. The policy also contains this footnote:

> "*For traumatic instability, early surgery may be considered for individuals with large bone defects or individuals under age 35."

I am not relying on that footnote, because my records show I completed the full 12 weeks of conservative care the main criterion asks for. I mention it only for completeness.

Because the denial notice states a general imaging rationale rather than identifying which specific criterion my records failed, I ask the plan to tell me, in writing, exactly which criterion it applied and which document it found lacking. If any required component of the documentation was missing from the submission, I would like the chance to supply it.

## What I am asking for

I ask that Blue Cross Blue Shield of Illinois overturn the denial dated 2026-08-11 (reference POC-A755F8592E-91154) and authorize CPT 29806. My surgeon has documented that this procedure is medically necessary, and the records establish each of the criteria quoted above, including the MRI finding the policy requires.

If the plan upholds the denial in whole or in part, I ask for a written explanation identifying the specific criterion not met and the records reviewed, along with a copy of the clinical review criteria used and information about my further appeal rights, including any right to external review.

I understand my appeal must be received by 2027-02-07, which is 180 days from the date of the notice. I am submitting this appeal by mail to the appeal address printed on my denial letter. I can also be reached through Blue Access for Members at bcbsil.com or by calling the number on my member ID card.

Documents enclosed:
- Copy of the denial notice dated 2026-08-11
- MR arthrogram report dated 2026-07-08
- Physical therapy discharge note (2026-04-03 to 2026-06-26, 16 visits)
- Office notes documenting examination findings and dislocation history
- [Any additional records to be listed]

Thank you for your time and for taking another look at this.

Sincerely,

\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_
Taylor Carter
